name: ALGOL 68
year_note: The Final Report was adopted by IFIP Working Group 2.1 on 20 December 1968 and published in 1969; the Revised Report was completed in 1973 and published in 1975. The first implementation, ALGOL 68-R, ran in 1970.
tagline: ALGOL's ambitious, orthogonal successor: user-defined operators, tagged unions, parallel clauses and a two-level grammar.
summary: ALGOL 68 was IFIP Working Group 2.1's successor to ALGOL 60, designed around orthogonality: a small set of independent concepts — modes (types), coercions and references — that combine freely. Every construct yields a value, programmers can declare new operators with their own priorities, and the language provided structures, tagged unions, heap storage with garbage collection and parallel clauses. It was defined with an unusually formal two-level (van Wijngaarden) grammar; its complexity limited adoption, but its ideas reached C, the Bourne shell and later languages.
history:
IFIP Working Group 2.1 spent the mid-1960s designing a successor to ALGOL 60. A proposal by Niklaus Wirth and Tony Hoare was judged too small an advance, and in a contentious process the group chose Adriaan van Wijngaarden's far more ambitious design; Wirth went on to build ALGOL W and later Pascal. The Final Report was adopted on 20 December 1968 over a Minority Report signed by Edsger Dijkstra, Tony Hoare and six other members who objected to its complexity.

The Royal Radar Establishment's ALGOL 68-R (1970) was the first working compiler, followed by ALGOL 68C at Cambridge and others. Stephen Bourne, who worked on ALGOL 68C, carried its if ... fi and case ... esac syntax into the Unix Bourne shell. A Revised Report (1973, published 1975) cleaned up the definition and remains the reference.

The language has since been revived by open-source implementations: Marcel van der Veer's interpreter Algol 68 Genie, first published in 2001, and ga68, a front end by Jose E. Marchesi that was merged into GCC in November 2025 as an experimental language for GCC 16.
innovations: Orthogonal design: modes, coercions and references combine without special cases
Expression-oriented syntax: every clause, including IF and CASE, yields a value
User-declared operators with programmable priorities, and overloading of existing ones
Type-safe united modes (tagged unions) inspected with conformity CASE clauses
The two-level van Wijngaarden grammar, which expressed context conditions in the syntax itself
PAR clauses and semaphores for parallel execution inside the language
Heap allocation with garbage collection in an ALGOL-family language

typing.notes: Modes are equivalent by structure, not by name. The syntactic context determines which implicit coercions apply (dereferencing, widening INT to REAL, uniting into a UNION, voiding), and united values can only be used after a conformity check.

influenced_by.note: Designed by IFIP WG 2.1 as the successor to ALGOL 60.

influenced_by_external.name: ALGOL Y
influenced_by_external.note: A more radical successor language discussed in WG 2.1 alongside the work that became ALGOL 68.

structured-control.note: IF ~ FI, CASE ~ ESAC and FOR/WHILE ~ DO ~ OD, all usable as expressions, with brief forms such as ( c | a | b ).

recursion.note: Recursive procedures and recursive modes (e.g. a list node holding a REF to its own mode).

algebraic-data-types.note: STRUCT modes are products and UNION modes are tagged sums, taken apart with conformity CASE clauses; alternatives are distinguished by mode rather than by named constructors.

structural-typing.note: Two MODE declarations with the same structure denote the same mode.

operator-overloading.note: OP declarations overload operators by operand modes, and PRIO sets the priority of new dyadic operators.

first-class-functions.note: PROC values can be stored, passed and returned, and routine texts such as (INT x) INT: x * x are anonymous functions.

closures.note: Routine texts capture their lexical environment, but scope rules forbid a routine from outliving the locals it uses; Algol 68 Genie adds partial parametrisation as an extension.

garbage-collection.note: HEAP generators allocate storage reclaimed by a garbage collector; LOC storage lives on the stack.

pointers.note: REF modes are typed references with NIL, but there is no pointer arithmetic or explicit deallocation.

milestones.event: Final Report adopted by IFIP WG 2.1 on 20 December, over a Minority Report
ALGOL 68-R, the first working compiler, at the Royal Radar Establishment
Algol 68 Genie released under the GNU GPL
ga68 front end merged into GCC as an experimental language (GCC 16)

trivia: Stephen Bourne reused ALGOL 68's if ... fi and case ... esac in the Unix shell and wrote its C source with macros giving it an ALGOL 68 look, a style nicknamed 'Bournegol'.
The Minority Report was signed by Edsger Dijkstra, Fraser Duncan, Jan Garwick, Tony Hoare, Brian Randell, Gerhard Seegmüller, Wlad Turski and Mike Woodger.

hello.dialect: ALGOL 68 Revised Report (Algol 68 Genie, UPPER stropping)
hello.notes: Keywords are bold symbols in the Report; Algol 68 Genie's default UPPER stropping writes them in capitals, leaving lower case for identifiers. print takes a row of values and layout routines such as newline. Unlike ALGOL 60, ALGOL 68 defined its standard I/O ('transput') in the Report itself.

factorial.dialect: ALGOL 68 Revised Report (Algol 68 Genie, UPPER stropping)
factorial.notes: The IF ... FI clause is an expression that yields the result; the brief form (n <= 1 | 1 | n * factorial(n - 1)) is equivalent. whole(x, 0) formats an integer in minimal width, whereas plain print would add a sign and padding.

fizzbuzz.dialect: ALGOL 68 Revised Report (Algol 68 Genie, UPPER stropping)
fizzbuzz.code:
FOR i TO 15 DO
   # IF ... FI is an expression: it yields the string to print #
   print((IF i MOD 15 = 0 THEN "FizzBuzz"
          ELIF i MOD 3 = 0 THEN "Fizz"
          ELIF i MOD 5 = 0 THEN "Buzz"
          ELSE whole(i, 0)
          FI, newline))
OD
fizzbuzz.expected_output:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
fizzbuzz.notes: FOR i TO 15 starts at 1 by default; any of a loop's FOR, FROM, BY, TO and WHILE parts may be omitted. The conditional clause yields the string that print consumes, and comments are delimited by # ... #.

higher-order.dialect: ALGOL 68 Revised Report (Algol 68 Genie, UPPER stropping)
higher-order.notes: There is no built-in map or filter, but PROC modes are first-class, so they are ordinary procedures taking routine texts such as (INT x) BOOL: NOT ODD x. n +:= 1 increments n and yields it, ys[1 : n] slices a row, and the brief conditional ( ... | " " | newline ) chooses the separator.

shapes.dialect: ALGOL 68 Revised Report (Algol 68 Genie, UPPER stropping)
shapes.notes: UNION(RECTANGLE, TRIANGLE) is a type-safe tagged union, and the conformity CASE clause dispatches on the value's actual mode while binding r or t — an early form of algebraic data types with pattern matching. Fields are selected with width OF r.

signature.title: User-defined operators and priorities
signature.dialect: ALGOL 68 Revised Report (Algol 68 Genie, UPPER stropping)
signature.notes: ALGOL 68 originated user-definable operators: OP gives + and * new meanings for the VEC mode (resolved by operand modes), PRIO declares the priority (1–9) of the brand-new dyadic operator DOT, and monadic operators such as SHOW need no priority. Structure displays like (1, 2) are coerced to VEC by context.

toolchains.name: Algol 68 Genie (a68g)
toolchains.notes: Interpreter; diagnostics such as warnings about hidden declarations go to stderr.

runtime.notes: All six snippets were verified with Algol 68 Genie 3.1.2. GCC 16's experimental ga68 front end is a native-code alternative.
